Among famines in the second half of the 20th century, however, the “Great Leap” Famine from 1959 to 61 in China stands out
as the worst in recorded history, precipitated by profound failure in centrally planned economic development and veiled by lack
of transparent governance and a free press. Following several years of land reform that marginally increased grain production
after birth of the Peoples’ Republic, Mao Zedong’s inconsistent farm collectivization policies, rural industrialization schemes
and internecine politics destroyed peasant incentives and reduced crop output amid pronounced exaggerations in crop yields
(Dikötter, 2010). State-sponsored vigilante groups extracting grain from farmers for urban centers, and state controls on food
grain transport, access, purchase and taxation preconditioned China for an inevitable collapse of it’s food system when pushed
by Mao to further accelerate production in 1958. The ensuing famine led to an estimated 18–32 million Chinese deaths in 1959–
62, implicating a vital role for unbiased journalism that can alert and hold government accountable to mount prevention.
